BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Continued good agreement amongst forecast guidance that an active weather pattern will be in place throughout the week and into next weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Milder tonight under increasing clouds.
- Light rain and mountain snow Monday afternoon through Tuesday morning, mainly in northern areas.
- Windy Monday afternoon in open southern areas.
- Continuing chance of light rain and snow showers in northern areas Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Upper low from the Gulf of Alaska was near the WA coast early this afternoon, with surface cold front already inland, and high clouds over all of WA and OR. The upper low center is forecast inland along 45N tonight and Monday, a little north of yesterday's predicted track. This change means less pcpn for our CWA Monday and Monday night, with new estimates .20 to .40 inch in northern mountains, .10 to .20 inch in northern valleys and southern mountains, and less than .10 inch in southern valleys. South of the Snake Basin will probably stay dry. The system will be cold enough, though, for a dusting to 2 inches of snow in northern areas above 5000 feet. Marginal instability will also support a slight (10-15%) chance of weak thunderstorms in Harney County and the central Idaho mountains Monday. Monday afternoon also looks windy in open areas of southeast OR and southern ID, with west/southwest gusts 25 to 30 mph. Low temps tonight will be milder than the previous two nights under increasing clouds. High temps Monday will get into the mid 60s in southern ID before the cold front arrives. Northern and western areas will be 4 to 8 degrees cooler than today with the front already past. Partial clearing Monday night will allow lows Tuesday morning 5 to 10 degrees colder than tonight, with patchy fog toward morning. Another weak upper low will approach from western WA Tuesday and maintain clouds and chance of rain and snow showers in northern areas through the day, then clearing Tuesday night except in the far north where a chance of rain and snow showers will continue into Wednesday. The clearing skies elsewhere will allow colder low temps Wednesday morning and slightly warmer high temps Wednesday afternoon.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Continued good agreement amongst forecast guidance that an active weather pattern will be in place throughout the week and into next weekend. Guidance is narrowing focus on a more impactful low pressure system for the weekend, with the best chances for precipitation on Saturday Night and Sunday. Temperatures are expected to remain at or near normal for the period.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: There is still considerable uncertainty in next weekend's weather as seen in the ensemble output. There are indications a subtropical push could occur as early as Friday but the main impacts of this first wave would likely stay southeast of our forecast area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Another round of showers and even a couple thunderstorms tonight into early Monday morning.
- Generally light snow accumulations in the mountains, with minor travel impacts over some of the high passes through early Monday morning.
- Warming trend and mostly dry much of upcoming week.
- Unsettled weather potentially returning next weekend, but odds favor western and southern Colorado once again.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Satellite shows the upper level low over northeast Utah, with a couple shortwaves rotating around it. The most impressive one was now lifting quickly northward through central and eastern New Mexico on the heels of an 80 kt upper level speed max. Other showers and thunderstorms were developing in the slightly unstable and still moist airmass over western and central Colorado ahead of the upper level trough. It appears both of those features will generate the highest coverage of showers at least early tonight as there is ascent associated with each. That supports the eastern plains and most of the mountains, while the I-25 Corridor would see lower but still scattered coverage of mainly light showers.

Later tonight into early Monday morning, another speed max is forecast to eject from the base of the trough as it lifts into the Central and Northern High Plains. By the time that shortwave organizes again, the main precipitation shield is expected to be mostly over the northern and far eastern plains. We still have about a 30-50% chance of seeing a half inch of rain over the northern tier of counties, with those odds decreasing rather quickly to the south including most of the I-70 Corridor and Denver metro. In fact, our deterministic forecast (essentially 50th percentile) has less than a tenth of an inch for Denver metro area and only about a 50% chance of a measurable rain. For the mountains, we still think the northern tier of mountains (e.g. Park/northern Gore/Medicine Bow Ranges and Rocky Mountain National Park) would see a 1-4" snow, while the rest of the mountains including the I-70 Corridor through Summit County would see a dusting to 2". Brief heavier showers and colder temperatures overnight would allow some travel impacts on some of the higher passes, but overall a pretty light snow event.

Precipitation will quickly end behind the trough passage early Monday morning, with some sunshine returning. However, it may take some time to clear as the plains will be shrouded in low clouds and areas of fog in the morning, and mixing will be slow given weak boundary layer winds and stronger inversions. Thus, another cool day with temperatures generally at or slightly below seasonal normals is on tap for Monday.

For Tuesday, a stronger zonal flow will develop, leading to dry weather, more sunshine, and warmer temperatures due to increasing downslope. Breezy conditions will develop over the mountains and high valleys with moderate pressure gradients in place. Similar conditions can be expected Wednesday and Thursday, with temperatures warming a couple more degrees and highs pushing near 70F on the plains and I-25 Corridor.

There is still considerable uncertainty in next weekend's weather as seen in the ensemble output. There are indications a subtropical push could occur as early as Friday but the main impacts of this first wave would likely stay southeast of our forecast area. A larger trough along with a possible pineapple connection is forecast to move into the southwest U.S. next weekend, but models are all over the place regarding it's eventual track and evolution. At this point, it still looks like areas over southern and western Colorado would be most prone for more significant precipitation.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Downslope winds should result in relatively mild temperatures for this time of the year Tuesday through Thursday, but not quite as warm as it has been prior to this weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread rain and mountain snowfall expected today and Monday as a central Pacific system lifts northeast across the region.
- Near normal temperatures and a bit warmer by Tuesday through Thursday, but the next Pacific system will be approaching from the eastern Pacific later in the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: What a difference a day will make as we see a more active weather pattern through Monday morning across the CWA as a stout upper level low moves from the Desert Southwest into the region. But first, lets take a quick look at today's temperatures with highs west of I-25 topping out in the lower 50s and lower to upper 40s east of the corridor. While lows tonight dip into the lower to mid 30s. Switching gears a bit and taking a look at the upper levels, initially we have a cut off low over the Desert Southwest while we sit under a southwesterly flow regime with a ridge to our east across the Mississippi Valley. As we progress through this afternoon, the cut off low will lift northeast and as it does so, the flow aloft over the CWA will become difluent, this combined with a plume of Pacific moisture and favorable ascent will support increased precipitation chances across the CWA by the late afternoon hours through the overnight into Monday morning.

Lets take a closer look at today through Monday morning, the low over the Southwest will continue to lift northeast closer to our CWA. Guidance indicates a surge of moisture ahead of this system, with ensemble members having PWATs above and around the 98th percentile. With adequate forcing, moderate rainfall looks to be a possibility. So, with ingredients in place, this looks like a scenario where up to 0.5" of rainfall, locally higher amounts, are possible across southeast Wyoming. With the best dynamics setting up over the Nebraska Panhandle, many locations there have the best chances of seeing 1.0" of precipitation. With this system moving in, especially in the afternoon hours, it is not out of the realm of possibility to see a few embedded weak thunderstorms as there is some instability in place, albeit a very slight chance. The coverage with regards to the rain showers will initially be scattered in nature then become more widespread this afternoon into the evening/overnight hours, when the heaviest of the precipitation is expected due to the influx of Pacific moisture. As we head into the overnight hours, the upper level low will slide northeast across the CWA. As it continues to lift off to the northeast Monday morning, rain showers will linger across the Nebraska Panhandle with clearing off to the west. This clearing will continue through the day as the system lifts out of the region, from a west to east. Most of the precipitation should remain as all rain, but for the late evening hours through the overnight can't rule out a few snow flakes mixing in. Not expecting any accumulations at lower elevations due to the warm soil temperatures, but higher elevation may see sub-advisory snowfall, with amounts on the order of 5.0" or less.

Expect slightly cooler temperatures Monday to hang on east of the I- 25 corridor as highs will only top out in the lower to mid 40s across the Nebraska Panhandle while elsewhere highs will approach the low 50s. Looking west of I-25, highs will top out into the lower to mid 50s. Lows Monday night will tank into the lower 30s, to near freezing.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: No major changes in the long term period, please see previous discussion...

Medium to long range models in reasonable agreement through late week, with a period of quiet weather expected for southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska during the middle of the week. Models show moderate southwesterly flow across the area with the polar jet staying north of the Front Range, and the subtropical jet staying well to the south over Texas and northern Mexico. We're kind of in- between these two separate storm tracks for most of the week with mostly quiet weather expected and near or slightly above average temperatures. A pair of potent Pacific shortwave troughs are forecast to impact the area late this weekend and early next week, with the second one likely missing southern Wyoming and remaining north of the area Tuesday. Models show a surface "cold front" rapidly moving east and clipping the forecast area to the north. However, all this front will do is shift low to midlevel winds into the west and increase wind speeds on Tuesday and Tuesday night...producing somewhat warmer downslope winds for a bulk of the area, including the high plains. Will need to watch for High Wind criteria for the typical wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming since most models show 700mb winds increasing over 45 knots by Tuesday morning and remaining elevated through Tuesday night with a decent surface pressure gradient and some hint of brief mountain wave activity. At this time, in-house wind guidance shows probability of wind gusts over 55 MPH around 20% to 45% for Arlington, Bordeaux, and even some of the sub wind prone areas along Interstate 25 near Douglas. For now, increase wind speeds up to criteria but did not increase wind gusts over 60 MPH quite yet. Event should be pretty brief and not too widespread, and peak mid Tuesday morning. Models have backed off on winds Tuesday night/early Wednesday with a slight downward trend, so kept those winds lower for now.

Downslope winds should result in relatively mild temperatures for this time of the year Tuesday through Thursday, but not quite as warm as it has been prior to this weekend. Kept high temperatures in the upper 50s to upper 60s, warmest of the eastern plains below 5000 feet and coolest temperatures across Carbon and Albany counties. Peak temperatures should occur later in the week with highs approaching 70 degrees over the western Nebraska panhandle as an upper level ridge axis across the southern United States and the Gulf amplifies ahead of the next Pacific storm system. Model solutions begin to diverge at this time, which is to be expected nearly 7 days out, as potential long wave trough attempts to settle across the eastern Pacific Ocean with a potent storm system pushing inland and into the Great Basin Region by late next Saturday and into next Sunday. Will have to keep an eye on this storm later in the forecast period as some model solutions and ensembles show a decent amount of colder air along with a subtropical moisture tap from the central Pacific. This pattern typically favors lee-side low pressure systems and an active weather pattern for the Front Range.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: This low finally moves east of the Divide by Monday morning, with much drier conditions expected through the day Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flooding along the San Juan river is ongoing across portions of southeast Utah, and is expected to continue through late Monday.
- Scattered showers and storms will be capable of producing moderate rainfall that could result in additional local flooding through Sunday evening.
- Mountain passes could see minor snowfall amounts on roadways by Monday morning.
- Monday through Thursday is expected to be mostly dry, but another impactful system is possible next weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Drier air tries to push in from the southwest during today as the low finally starts to lift northeast. We are still expecting showers and storms during the afternoon and evening. These storms will be capable of producing brief moderate rain, frequent lightning, small hail, and gusty winds. Colder air in the wake of the front and lingering moisture will allow for light mountain rain and snow showers to linger Sunday night into Monday. Again, little snow accumulation is expected, but passes could once again be slippery Monday morning, especially along the Central and Northern Divide.

This low finally moves east of the Divide by Monday morning, with much drier conditions expected through the day Monday. A quick moving clipper will just brush our northern border Monday night into Tuesday, with the potential for some light rain and snow showers over the higher terrain of the eastern Uintas and Northern Colorado Divide. Behind this clipper, zonal flow takes control, bringing mostly quiet conditions and gradually warming temperatures through the back half of the work week. Highs start out 5-10 degrees below normal Sunday through Tuesday, climbing to near-normal by the Wednesday-Thursday time period. By Friday, flow aloft shifts to a moister southwesterly direction in response to a low deepening off the West Coast, bringing increased cloud cover and a slight cooldown. Model agreement is poor beyond this point, but there are indications that we could see a return to cooler and unsettled conditions by next weekend.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: For the weekend...Another trough is forecast to move across the Western CONUS. Both the primary deterministic guidance products (EC/GFS) show this trough development, but vary in the intensity and location of the trough.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Another 18 hours of showers, then we dry out.
- Mainly dry this upcoming week, then another potentially active event for later next weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: With the mid level trough still to our west, lifting northeast, a couple more rounds of showers will be likely across the region the rest of this afternoon into late evening. Some of the showers will produce heavy rain, but should be relatively quick moving. The best chance of showers over the most populated area (Springs/Pueblo) will occur mainly this evening (6 pm-midnight).
The activity should clear the forecast areas and move into KS by Sunrise tomorrow.
Tomorrow should be mostly sunny and dry predominantly dry, The only showers may occur in far SE CO. Max temps tomorrow should be in the mid 60s plains and low 50s valleys.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Tuesday through Thursday will be dry. Max temps should be in the U60s/L70s plains with 50s in the valleys.
By Friday, temps will be similar to the days prior, but we will see a chance of showers over the San Juans and possibly the far southeast plains.

For the weekend...Another trough is forecast to move across the Western CONUS. Both the primary deterministic guidance products (EC/GFS) show this trough development, but vary in the intensity and location of the trough. GFS is more gung-ho with a stronger system while EC is farther north and quicker. As it stands now, it appears the mountains along the divide should get precip with this system, and since these systems appear colder, we should see more snow than rain the the mtns. \/Hodanish

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: A more substantial storm starts to emerge towards the end of the week and into the weekend as the aforementioned broad trough starts to shift further south and begins to pull in deep moisture from the southern jet stream.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Weak cold frontal passage across northern Utah Monday night will bring a little bit of valley rain and mountain snow in addition to a cool down.
- A more substantial storm arrives by the end of the week into the weekend with the potential for widespread precipitation that could increase the risk of flash flooding.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: An area of low pressure is centered across northeastern Utah with light rain and snow showers along the terrain of central and northern Utah. Snow levels have been hovering around 9000 feet with accumulating snow on non-paved surfaces observed at Wolf Creek Pass, although this snow has been melting as the snow showers move out. Not expecting more than a quick dusting under heavier showers at elevation. A few lightning strikes are possible this afternoon as conditions de-stabilize slightly, but most of this activity will remain in the form of brief light showers across the terrain of central and northeastern Utah.

This low will move out of the area tonight with shortwave ridging moving into the region tomorrow that will help temperatures rise back into the 60s across most valley locations and low 70s across lower Washington county. These temperatures will trend lower by 5-8 degrees across northern Utah and SW Wyoming after the passage of a shallow cold front Monday evening. Guidance has trended down on QPF totals as hi-res guidance comes into frame. Most of the hi-res guidance keeps all of the precipitation to our north, but the NBM 50th percentile still has 0.1-0.2" of QPF near the Idaho border with lesser amounts as you head down the Wasatch before tapering off to nothing basically south of Utah County. A quick dusting to an inch of snow will be possible with the frontal passage as snow levels get down to 6000-7000 feet.

We will remain in a zonal flow with a broad trough across the PNW that will keep conditions mostly dry with near normal temperatures. Being on the periphery of this trough will keep the door open for some grazing shortwaves. Guidance is starting to pick up on one of these Tuesday night that could bring another brief grazing of valley rain and mountain snow across northern Utah/SW Wyoming, but this will be brief with limited precipitation totals likely. The NBM 90th percentile gets as high as 0.5" with this round of precipitation, but the 50th keeps totals <0.25".

A more substantial storm starts to emerge towards the end of the week and into the weekend as the aforementioned broad trough starts to shift further south and begins to pull in deep moisture from the southern jet stream. The timing of this will be key to when and where the heaviest precipitation sets up. Guidance seems to have slowed down today with a bulk of the activity holding off until the ladder half of the weekend as opposed to the first half that was being advertised the past couple of days. 50% of the ensemble members keeps this trough across the west for several days. This will increase our risk of flash flooding, particularly is the trough and heaviest moisture tap merge across the Great Basin.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
